why: 50 mg diphenhydramine reliably raises subjective drowsiness within 1-2 h; that is why it is sold as a sleep aid.
source: Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350 (diphenhydramine vs loratadine, sedation and performance); Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203 (review of H1 antihistamines)

why: Blocking brain H1 receptors removes histamine's wake-promoting signal, so alertness drops clearly.
source: Yanai K, Tashiro M 2007, Pharmacol Ther 113:1 (H1 receptor occupancy PET and sedation); Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350

why: 50 mg impairs attention, reaction time and simulated driving, in one study more than a blood alcohol of 0.1%, often without people noticing how impaired they are.
source: Weiler JM et al. 2000, Ann Intern Med 132:354 (Iowa driving simulator: diphenhydramine vs fexofenadine vs alcohol)

why: In ordinary (non-drug-using) volunteers 50 mg tends to feel slightly unpleasant and dull rather than euphoric; liking is reported mainly by people with a drug-use history.
source: Preston KL et al. 1992, J Pharmacol Exp Ther 262:707 (abuse liability of diphenhydramine); Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350 (mood scales)

why: Sedating antihistamines calm mild tension (hydroxyzine is an approved anxiolytic), but diphenhydramine's own anxiolytic effect is poorly studied.
source: Guaiana G et al. 2010, Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD006815 (hydroxyzine for GAD); Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203

why: At the normal 50 mg dose people feel drowsy and foggy but do not get hallucinations or distorted perception.
source: Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203; Radovanovic D et al. 2000, Hum Exp Toxicol 19:489 (toxicity only well above therapeutic doses)

why: Around 300 mg and above, the anticholinergic action produces confusion, delirium and often realistic hallucinations (seeing insects, talking to people who are not there).
source: Radovanovic D et al. 2000, Hum Exp Toxicol 19:489 (diphenhydramine overdose, 136 cases: delirium/psychosis rises above ~300 mg); Scharman EJ et al. 2006, Clin Toxicol 44:205 (AAPCC guideline)

why: At 200 mg sedation and anticholinergic memory impairment combine into marked confusion and poor attention.
source: Scharman EJ et al. 2006, Clin Toxicol 44:205; Tejera CA et al. 1994, Am J Psychiatry 151:1381 (anticholinergic delirium from OTC antihistamines)

why: Taken at bedtime it adds clear drowsiness on top of normal evening sleep pressure and shortens time to fall asleep a little.
source: Morin CM et al. 2005, Sleep 28:1465 (diphenhydramine for insomnia, RCT); Kudo Y, Kurihara M 1990, J Clin Pharmacol 30:1041

why: With a half-life of about 8-9 h, a bedtime dose is still partly in the blood next morning and many people feel groggy ('hangover').
source: Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350; Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203; Paton DM, Webster DR 1985, Clin Pharmacokinet 10:477 (half-life)

why: Next-morning reaction time and divided attention are often still measurably impaired after a 50 mg bedtime dose.
source: Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350; Verster JC, Volkerts ER 2004, CNS Drug Rev 10:45 (antihistamines and driving)

why: Tolerance to the sedative effect develops within about 3-4 days of regular dosing, so after weeks the sleep effect is largely gone.
source: Richardson GS et al. 2002, J Clin Psychopharmacol 22:511 (tolerance to daytime sedative effects of diphenhydramine within 4 days)

why: Long-term H1 blockade is linked to more appetite and weight gain (as with cyproheptadine and some antipsychotics), but data for diphenhydramine itself are sparse.
source: Ratliff JC et al. 2010, Obesity 18:2398 (H1 antihistamine use and obesity); Kroeze WK et al. 2003, Neuropsychopharmacology 28:519 (H1 affinity predicts weight gain)

why: A single dose of donepezil does not reliably improve attention or memory in healthy people.
source: Repantis D et al. 2010, Pharmacol Res 61:473 (systematic review: AChE inhibitors for neuroenhancement in healthy individuals)

why: Weeks of donepezil give healthy adults at most tiny, inconsistent gains (one pilot simulator study) and sometimes slight impairment; it is not a brain booster for normal brains.
source: Repantis D et al. 2010, Pharmacol Res 61:473; Yesavage JA et al. 2002, Neurology 59:123; Beglinger LJ et al. 2005, J Clin Psychopharmacol 25:159

why: Extra acetylcholine in the gut causes nausea and loss of appetite, the commonest side effects, especially when starting.
source: Birks JS, Harvey RJ 2018, Cochrane Database Syst Rev CD001190 (donepezil adverse events: nausea, anorexia); Aricept prescribing information

why: Alcohol and diphenhydramine add their sedative effects, which is why labels warn against combining them.
source: Burns M, Moskowitz H 1980, Clin Pharmacol Ther 28:784 (antihistamine + alcohol psychomotor effects); Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203

why: Drowsiness starts within an hour, peaks around 1-3 h when blood levels peak, and fades over 4-8 h.
source: Paton DM, Webster DR 1985, Clin Pharmacokinet 10:477 (Tmax ~2 h, t1/2 ~8 h); Carruthers SG et al. 1978, Clin Pharmacol Ther 23:375

why: Loss of alertness follows the blood level: onset within an hour, peak at 1-3 h, mostly gone after 4-8 h.
source: Carruthers SG et al. 1978, Clin Pharmacol Ther 23:375 (plasma levels vs sedation); Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203

why: Measured performance impairment tends to outlast the feeling of sleepiness, so people feel fine before they are fine.
source: Weiler JM et al. 2000, Ann Intern Med 132:354; Verster JC, Volkerts ER 2004, CNS Drug Rev 10:45

why: A double dose has the same onset but lasts somewhat longer because levels stay above the sedating threshold longer.
source: Paton DM, Webster DR 1985, Clin Pharmacokinet 10:477; Carruthers SG et al. 1978, Clin Pharmacol Ther 23:375

why: Anticholinergic delirium after an overdose builds over a few hours and can last a day or more because absorption is slowed and elimination is long.
source: Radovanovic D et al. 2000, Hum Exp Toxicol 19:489; Scharman EJ et al. 2006, Clin Toxicol 44:205

why: Donepezil peaks in blood at 3-4 h and has a ~70 h half-life, so nausea appears within hours and can linger.
source: Rogers SL, Friedhoff LT 1998, Br J Clin Pharmacol 46 Suppl 1:1 (donepezil pharmacokinetics); Aricept prescribing information

why: At steady state donepezil blocks roughly 20-40% of brain acetylcholinesterase, which in animals raises cortical acetylcholine roughly 1.5-3-fold; no direct human measurement exists.
source: Kuhl DE et al. 2000, Neurology 55:1129 (PET: ~27% cortical AChE inhibition); Kosasa T et al. 1999, Eur J Pharmacol 380:101 (rat cortical ACh microdialysis)

why: A single dose reaches only a fraction of steady-state levels (long half-life, slow build-up), so the acute rise is smaller than with daily use.
source: Rogers SL, Friedhoff LT 1998, Br J Clin Pharmacol 46 Suppl 1:1; Kosasa T et al. 1999, Eur J Pharmacol 380:101

why: Nicotine stimulates nicotinic receptors on cholinergic and glutamate terminals and raises cortical acetylcholine release in animals; human cigarette doses are smaller.
source: Summers KL, Giacobini E 1995, Neurochem Res 20:753; Arnold HM et al. 2003, Neuropsychopharmacology 28:1749 (nicotine and prefrontal ACh)

why: Two opposing actions: muscarinic blockade of autoreceptors tends to raise acetylcholine release, while H1 blockade removes histamine's excitation of cholinergic cells; the level changes little, but its signal is blocked.
source: Kubo N et al. 1987, Jpn J Pharmacol 43:277 (antimuscarinic affinity of antihistamines); Khateb A et al. 1995, Neuroscience 69:495 (histamine excites basal forebrain cholinergic neurons)

why: Benzodiazepines strengthen GABA inhibition of basal-forebrain cholinergic neurons and lower cortical/hippocampal acetylcholine release in animal studies.
source: Moore H, Sarter M, Bruno JP 1993, Neurosci Lett 153:233; Imperato A et al. 1994, Brain Res 646:173

why: Caffeine blocks adenosine A1 receptors that normally brake acetylcholine release and raises prefrontal and hippocampal acetylcholine in rats.
source: Acquas E, Tanda G, Di Chiara G 2002, Neuropsychopharmacology 27:182

why: Diphenhydramine blocks the H1 receptor, not histamine release (which is controlled by H3 autoreceptors), so the histamine level itself barely changes while its wake signal is blocked.
source: Haas HL, Sergeeva OA, Selbach O 2008, Physiol Rev 88:1183 (histamine in the nervous system); Yanai K, Tashiro M 2007, Pharmacol Ther 113:1

why: Cortical acetylcholine is lowest in deep non-REM sleep, which dominates the first half of the night; it is high both when awake and in REM sleep later in the night.
source: Marrosu F et al. 1995, Brain Res 671:329 (cortical ACh in wake, NREM, REM); Jasper HH, Tessier J 1971, Science 172:601; Hasselmo ME 1999, Trends Cogn Sci 3:351

why: Acetylcholine is high throughout waking, but REM sleep in the early morning can reach similar or higher levels, so the peak time is not sharply defined.
source: Marrosu F et al. 1995, Brain Res 671:329; Lee MG et al. 2005, J Neurosci 25:4365 (basal forebrain cholinergic firing across wake/sleep)

why: Histamine neurons fire steadily only during waking, so brain histamine is high across the active day.
source: Takahashi K, Lin JS, Sakai K 2006, J Neurosci 26:10292 (TMN histamine neurons wake-active); Haas HL, Sergeeva OA, Selbach O 2008, Physiol Rev 88:1183

why: Histamine neurons go silent in both non-REM and REM sleep, so histamine is low throughout the night (unlike acetylcholine, which rebounds in REM).
source: Strecker RE et al. 2002, Neuroscience 113:663 (hypothalamic histamine across sleep-wake in cats); Takahashi K et al. 2006, J Neurosci 26:10292

why: Sedation increases with dose between 25-100 mg.
source: Carruthers SG et al. 1978, Clin Pharmacol Ther 23:375 (dose-related sedation); Kudo Y, Kurihara M 1990, J Clin Pharmacol 30:1041

why: Tolerance to the sleepy effect builds within days, so a regular user gets far less drowsiness than a first-time user.
source: Richardson GS et al. 2002, J Clin Psychopharmacol 22:511

why: Adding alcohol to diphenhydramine makes the sedation clearly stronger.
source: Burns M, Moskowitz H 1980, Clin Pharmacol Ther 28:784; product labelling (FDA OTC drug facts: avoid alcohol)

why: Hallucinations and delirium appear only at overdoses, not at the standard sleep-aid dose.
source: Radovanovic D et al. 2000, Hum Exp Toxicol 19:489; Scharman EJ et al. 2006, Clin Toxicol 44:205

why: The next-morning grogginess is real but smaller than the sedation at peak blood levels.
source: Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350; Paton DM, Webster DR 1985, Clin Pharmacokinet 10:477

why: 50 mg diphenhydramine is a strongly sedating dose, whereas 5 mg diazepam is a low anxiolytic dose with only mild daytime drowsiness in most people; direct head-to-head data are scarce.
source: Simons FER 2004, NEJM 351:2203; Woods JH, Katz JL, Winger G 1992, Pharmacol Rev 44:151 (benzodiazepine dose-effects); Kay GG et al. 1997, Arch Intern Med 157:2350
